A user who self-hosted Sentry said each release added more containers and consumed more memory until they couldn't run anything on their 32GB server except Sentry. They evaluated GlitchTip and Bugsink, found them similar, and chose GlitchTip.
A team running both Sentry and GlitchTip during an evaluation said GlitchTip has "so many bugs vs sentry," but they are trying to stick with it because it's much lighter.

A user with a small user base (<1000 users) said Sentry did not make sense for them. GlitchTip lacks some Sentry functionality but has everything they need, and has run in production for a year without problems.

GlitchTip replaced a self-hosted Sentry 9.x ("pre-Clickhouse madness"); migration was just updating the DSN in configs. The UI is a bit buggy and 'resolve' doesn't always work, but it does 99% of what Sentry did with 10% of the effort needed to maintain a modern Sentry setup.

A user who says they love Sentry found that for a growing business its features are more nice-to-have than critical. They noted it's easy to rack up a monthly bill on hosted services, and wished for a simpler, lightweight version to self-host when traffic is low. They also credited Sentry's self-hosting option as an escape hatch from full vendor lock-in.
An Amazon commenter said many developers at Amazon love(d) using Sentry, and one contributed a small PR back to the project.
Finding django-db-log (Sentry's origin) was a game changer. Errors-as-emails didn't scale across many Django sites, and having historical error data "made my code so much tighter."
A user who has interacted with Sentry staff said building for developers is not easy and thinks Sentry is "doing great in that front."
Sentry is source-available under the BSL; you can still run it for your company for free "if you feel like managing all of the infra it requires."

A commenter who built their own symbolicator said competitors such as Embrace use Sentry's open-source Symbolicator, which represents months of highly specialized work. They noted few if any outside contributions to it, and argued people underappreciate how much of Sentry is given away.

"We're huge fans of Sentry and have it deeply integrated in our products." The open source code let them see exactly what was happening for advanced integrations instead of relying on docs (which are also great). Despite the BSL change, they'll keep using Sentry and remain customers.
A happy Sentry user on the cloud offering in their early stages said it's good to know they can host their own instance if they ever "crumble under the costs."

A user who has run self-hosted Sentry at work for a couple of years, and the SaaS product for freelance work, said it has "worked fantastically" and is "rock-solid once running, I never worry about it." Self-hosted releases take time to appear after SaaS launches.

A user who was planning to implement Sentry for a side project called the BSL relicense very disappointing. Because they refuse to rely on closed-source software, they'll now find an alternative or use an old version.

Critic of the relicense: Sentry is no longer open source at all; people can only collaborate on three-year-old versions or a fork of the last open source release. They called this disappointing and worried more companies will follow.
